integrity_statement: All fifteen foundation sources clear the journal gate and were reviewed from complete publisher text or a complete author/institutional manuscript reconciled to the published DOI. Abstract-only records, search snippets, press summaries, and working papers without a qualifying journal publication do not count. Academic quantities remain prompt-time reasoning examples and never become current platform facts.

foundation_admissions.title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 53-page Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis author manuscript reconciled to the published INFORMS record

verified_extraction.claim_path: representative person-level use -> frequency and work-hours intensity -> reported task assistance and time savings
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Two nationally representative 2024 U.S. surveys totaling more than 10,000 respondents age 18-64; employed-worker denominators are separated from all-adult denominators
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Use and implied productivity potential vary by occupation, industry, education, age, and firm climate
limitations: Self-reported use and time savings are not instrumented production outcomes
Late-2024 conditions do not describe later model capabilities or current platform data
Worker-reported use is not equivalent to employer deployment

foundation_admissions.title: AI adoption in America: Who, what, and where

whole_text_audit.access: Complete Census/NBER institutional manuscript reconciled to Wiley publication

verified_extraction.claim_path: production-use definition -> establishment/firm adoption -> size-weighted diffusion -> concentration among large firms
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: 2018 Annual Business Survey sent to roughly 850,000 U.S. firms and linked to Census longitudinal business data; firm-weighted and employment-weighted rates are distinct
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Adoption is much higher among very large firms and varies with firm age, owner education and experience, industry, and geography
limitations: Measures five pre-generative-AI technologies around 2017-2018
Cross-sectional adoption patterns do not establish productivity effects
A firm-weighted rate cannot be compared directly with an employment-weighted rate

foundation_admissions.title: Artificial intelligence adoption and system-wide change

whole_text_audit.access: Complete Wiley article text and complete author record

verified_extraction.claim_path: task-level prediction improvement -> increased decision variation -> interaction with organizational interdependence -> coordination or modular redesign
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Formal multi-decision organizational model, not an empirical adoption estimate
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Interdependencies can impede adoption without coordination yet raise adoption value when coordination mechanisms exist
limitations: Theoretical propositions are not observed firm outcomes
The result depends on modeled interdependence and coordination costs
Task-level capability cannot be treated as system-level implementation

foundation_admissions.title: Experimental evidence on the productivity effects of generative artificial intelligence

whole_text_audit.access: Complete MIT author manuscript reconciled to Science publication

verified_extraction.claim_path: random access to ChatGPT -> task completion time and blind quality scores -> within-task productivity and distribution
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: 453 college-educated professionals completing incentivized mid-level professional writing tasks
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Lower initial performers gain more, compressing the measured productivity distribution
limitations: Short, bounded writing tasks are not jobs or complete workflows
Participants and tasks do not represent the whole workforce
Time and quality gains do not directly establish firm revenue, profit, wages, or employment

whole_text_audit.access: Complete Oxford Academic article HTML and replication record

verified_extraction.claim_path: production deployment -> suggestion access and adherence -> speed, resolution, quality, learning, and work-experience outcomes
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Staggered rollout to 5,172 customer-support agents at one Fortune 500 software firm and its contractors
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Large gains accrue to novice and lower-skill agents; top agents see little speed gain and a small quality decline
limitations: One firm, one occupation, and one tool
Medium-run partial-equilibrium evidence does not identify wages or aggregate labor demand
Attrition estimates lack worker fixed effects and warrant more caution

foundation_admissions.title: AI, Skill, and Productivity: The Case of Taxi Drivers

verified_extraction.claim_path: voluntary predictive-AI use -> customer-search time -> driver productivity by prior skill
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: 520 Yokohama taxi drivers offered a 29-day free trial; search time is the primary outcome
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Average search-time improvement is concentrated among lower-skill drivers, with near-zero effect for higher-skill drivers
limitations: Short trial in one city and occupation
Voluntary take-up creates selection addressed but not eliminated by design and IV checks
Search-time gains need not translate one-for-one into daily income or labor demand

foundation_admissions.title: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content

whole_text_audit.access: Complete open-access article through PubMed Central and Science Advances

verified_extraction.claim_path: access to one or five AI-generated ideas -> individual story ratings -> cross-story similarity
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: 293 writers and 600 blinded evaluators in a short-story experiment
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Writers with lower baseline creativity receive the largest individual gains; highly creative writers are not supercharged
limitations: Short stories are not firm innovation or commercial products
Uniform AI inputs and task design may contribute to homogenization
Higher ratings do not establish downstream market value

foundation_admissions.title: The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers

whole_text_audit.access: Complete MIT/Microsoft author manuscript reconciled to INFORMS publication

verified_extraction.claim_path: random coding-assistant access -> actual take-up -> completed development tasks
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Three workplace randomized trials totaling 4,867 developers at Microsoft, Accenture, and a Fortune 100 firm
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Less-experienced developers adopt more and obtain larger estimated gains; separate experiments are noisy
limitations: Pooled estimate masks cross-company imprecision and heterogeneity
Completed tasks do not fully measure code quality, maintainability, or business value
Access is not identical to sustained workflow integration

foundation_admissions.title: Artificial intelligence, firm growth, and product innovation

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 89-page author manuscript reconciled to the open-access JFE record and replication package

verified_extraction.claim_path: AI-skilled labor investment proxy -> later sales, employment, valuation, and innovation -> firm and industry distribution
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: U.S. public and private firms observed through worker resumes, job postings, financial records, and innovation measures over 2010-2018
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Growth and product-innovation gains concentrate among ex-ante larger firms, increasing concentration
limitations: AI-skilled hiring is an investment proxy, not direct observation of deployed use
The instrument and no-pretrend tests support but do not make every estimate experimental
Firm growth can include business stealing and does not imply aggregate net growth

whole_text_audit.access: Complete KU Leuven institutional manuscript reconciled to Elsevier publication

verified_extraction.claim_path: surveyed AI use and intensity -> firm production-function estimates -> productivity association
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: German firm survey and panel data with multiple AI-use measures
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Results are tested across adoption indicator and intensity measures and under cross-sectional, panel, and IV specifications
limitations: Country and survey context constrain external validity
Positive significant estimates do not measure worker incidence or aggregate spillovers
Instrument validity and self-reported adoption remain material identification considerations

foundation_admissions.title: Occupational, industry, and geographic exposure to artificial intelligence: A novel dataset and its potential uses

whole_text_audit.access: Complete Wiley article text and Princeton repository record

verified_extraction.claim_path: AI application progress -> occupational abilities -> occupation exposure -> industry and geography aggregation
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Ten AI applications mapped to 52 O*NET abilities and then to occupation employment structures
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Exposure can be aggregated differently by occupation, industry, county, and firm workforce composition
limitations: Exposure is direction-neutral and cannot distinguish complementarity from substitution
The measure does not observe adoption, task change, wages, employment, or displacement
Aggregation inherits O*NET and employment-weighting assumptions

foundation_admissions.title: GPTs are GPTs: Labor market impact potential of LLMs

whole_text_audit.access: Complete Science PDF and author manuscript

verified_extraction.claim_path: task descriptions -> modeled time-saving capability under quality constraint -> occupation-level potential exposure
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: U.S. O*NET tasks evaluated under human and model rubrics for direct LLM and LLM-powered-software scenarios
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Potential exposure spans wage levels and is higher in many higher-income knowledge occupations
limitations: The paper explicitly does not predict adoption timing
Potential exposure is not observed use, automation, displacement, or employment loss
Results depend on task descriptions, capability thresholds, and modeled software complementarity

foundation_admissions.title: New Frontiers: The Origins and Content of New Work, 1940-2018

verified_extraction.claim_path: augmentation or automation innovation -> new work creation -> occupational employment and wagebill
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Eight decades of U.S. job titles linked to Census microdata and patent-text measures
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: New-work creation shifts from middle-paid production and clerical work before 1980 toward high-paid professional and lower-paid services after 1980
limitations: Historical technology evidence is not a direct estimate of generative AI
Patent-text exposure measures innovation direction, not current deployment
Long-run occupation responses cannot be mapped mechanically onto short-run platform indicators

foundation_admissions.title: Artificial intelligence and jobs: evidence from US commuting zones

verified_extraction.claim_path: local industry composition and national AI adoption -> commuting-zone AI exposure -> employment-rate changes
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: U.S. commuting zones over 2000-2020 using a shift-share design
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Estimated employment effects are more negative in services, for lower-skill and production workers, and positive at the top of the wage distribution
limitations: Period largely predates mass-market generative AI
Shift-share estimates rely on exclusion and composition assumptions
Local relative effects need not equal national aggregate employment effects

verified_extraction.claim_path: share of tasks affected x task-level cost savings -> calibrated aggregate TFP and GDP path -> wage and inequality incidence
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Model-based calibration using published task-exposure and micro-productivity evidence over a ten-year horizon
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Hard-to-learn, context-dependent tasks reduce plausible aggregate gains relative to easy benchmark tasks; wage effects differ by demographic and occupational exposure
limitations: Calibration is a scenario, not an observed forecast track
Inputs inherit uncertainty from exposure measures and selected micro studies
Task cost savings are not automatically realized without adoption and complementary change

verified_atomic_observations.statement: Representative worker surveys require separate denominators for any use, work use, daily use, and assisted work hours.
Rapid extensive-margin adoption can coexist with shallow intensity when only a small share of total work hours is assisted.
Occupation, industry, age, education, and firm climate create material adoption heterogeneity.
Self-reported time savings are a transmission input, not verified firm productivity or aggregate output.
A production-use question yields a narrower adoption construct than testing, aspiration, invention, or AI-enabled product sales.
Firm-weighted adoption can be low while employment-weighted adoption is much higher because use concentrates in large employers.
Firm size, age, owner characteristics, sector, and geography shape diffusion and must survive any national average.
An adoption cross section maps diffusion but does not itself identify productivity, causality, or worker incidence.
Improving a prediction within one task can increase decision variation elsewhere in an interdependent organization.
Modularizing decisions can ease AI adoption while sacrificing synergies created by interdependence.
Coordination mechanisms can turn organizational interdependence from an adoption barrier into a source of value.
Task capability and system-wide productive use are different analytical states.
Randomized access on bounded professional writing tasks identifies a task treatment, not a complete job redesign.
Productivity assessment should carry both completion time and independently graded quality.
Larger gains among lower initial performers can compress within-task performance inequality.
A worker-task productivity effect cannot be promoted to firm revenue, employment, or aggregate TFP without added links.
A staggered production rollout provides stronger workflow evidence than a laboratory capability benchmark.
Worker effects vary sharply by prior skill and tenure, including possible quality declines among top performers.
Resolved issues per hour decomposes into handling time, concurrency, resolution, and quality rather than a single speed metric.
Medium-run gains in one firm do not determine wages, total labor demand, or longer-run equilibrium adjustment.
Actual voluntary use of predictive AI in a field setting links adoption to observed task productivity.
A prediction tool can substitute for a skill component and therefore benefit lower-skill workers more.
Search-time efficiency is a task outcome and should not be relabeled as daily income or total output.
Single-city and single-occupation evidence requires an explicit external-validity boundary.
Individual quality and collective output diversity are separate outcome dimensions that can move in opposite directions.
Baseline creativity conditions who benefits from AI-generated ideas.
An individually rational productivity aid can create a collective homogenization cost.
Deployment design and input uniformity are part of the treatment and limit generalization to configurable systems.
Randomized workplace trials across three firms improve external validity while retaining company-level heterogeneity.
Tool access, adoption, and completed tasks are sequentially distinct measurements.
Less-experienced developers can have both higher take-up and larger productivity gains.
Completed tasks omit maintainability, error costs, and business value unless those outcomes are measured separately.
AI-skilled employee resumes and postings measure firm investment, not direct deployed use.
AI investment is associated with sales, employment, valuation, and product innovation rather than only cost cutting.
AI-linked growth concentrating in initially large firms can increase industry concentration.
Firm growth may include business stealing, so firm estimates do not establish aggregate net growth.
Firm-survey adoption indicators and intensity measures provide distinct tests of the productivity relationship.
Cross-sectional, panel, and instrumental-variable estimates form an identification ladder rather than equivalent proof.
Country institutions, industrial mix, and survey definitions constrain external validity.
Firm productivity evidence does not reveal worker compensation, labor share, or aggregate spillovers by itself.
Occupational exposure can be constructed by mapping AI applications to the abilities used in occupations.
Occupation exposure can be aggregated to industries and geographies only through explicit employment weights.
Direction-neutral exposure cannot decide whether AI complements or substitutes for workers.
Exposure is neither adoption nor an observed employment, wage, productivity, or displacement outcome.
A task can be technically exposed under a time-and-quality rubric even when no worker or firm uses the tool.
Direct-model and software-augmented scenarios are modeled capability regimes, not observed adoption paths.
LLM exposure extends into higher-income knowledge work unlike many earlier automation measures.
Potential task impact must never be translated directly into jobs lost or a timetable for displacement.
Augmentation innovations create new work and raise occupational labor demand while automation innovations erode it.
The locus of new work changes across eras and skill groups, making historical averages regime-dependent.
Demand shocks and innovation direction jointly determine whether new tasks appear.
Automation and augmentation can rise together within occupations while exerting opposite labor-demand effects.
Local industry composition can transmit national technology adoption into heterogeneous commuting-zone employment effects.
Estimated employment incidence differs by sector, skill, production status, and wage rank.
A shift-share design requires explicit instrument and local-composition qualifications.
Negative local relative effects do not mechanically imply the same national aggregate employment effect.
Aggregate gains require both the share of tasks affected and the average cost saving on those tasks.
Easy-to-learn task evidence can overstate gains on context-dependent tasks with noisy objectives.
A calibrated ten-year TFP range is a scenario conditional on inputs, not an observed current outcome.
Adoption, complementary change, prices, demand, wages, and distribution mediate the path from task savings to macro outcomes.

anti_patterns_locked: Never use exposure as a synonym for adoption, automation, displacement, or job loss.
Never use any-use, weekly-use, daily-use, or assisted-hour shares interchangeably.
Never compare firm-weighted, employment-weighted, worker, seat, subscriber, or population denominators without naming them.
Never turn a task experiment into a claim about firm productivity, labor demand, or GDP.
Never turn firm growth into aggregate growth without accounting for selection, business stealing, entry, prices, and spillovers.
Never collapse speed, quality, cost, output, revenue, profit, wages, and welfare into one productivity claim.
Never erase heterogeneous effects by skill, experience, firm size, sector, occupation, geography, or adoption intensity.
Never describe a model calibration, scenario, or potential exposure estimate as an observed outcome.
Never insert academic quantities into a live Read as though they were current platform observations.
